title: Penitent acts are moral conditions, not physical causes of first grace
source_text: L. Et similiter, quamvis dicant actus poenitentiae, timoris, spei, & dilectionis, esse cum fidei actu dispositiones quasdam ad justificationem, non intelligunt propterea opera ejusmodi, proprie loquendo, justificationem, vel efficere, vel mereri. Non sunt enim, ex eorum mente, dispositiones physicae, quae propria sua virtute remissionem peccatorum, & justitiam novam efficiant, vel attingant: sed dispositiones solummodo morales, id est, conditiones, quae juxta divinam ordinationem, remissionem peccatorum, & justitiae habitualis donum, in nobis praecedere debent, & sine quibus Deus beneficia ista homini non vult, nec solet conferre, ut videre est apud Petrum a Sancto Joseph in Idea Theologiae Speculativae, lib. 4. cap. 9. Resolutione 3. nec etiam, ut ante ex ipso Concilio Tridentino probatum est, ullis operibus tribuunt vim promerendi gratiam justificationis, quae, ut notat idem Concilium, non est sola peccatorum remissio, sed & sanctificatio, & renovatio interioris hominis: quam remissionem & renovationem Theologi omnes Ecclesiae Romanae agnoscunt esse mere gratuitam, & nullis nostris actibus, aut dispositionibus ex justitia deberi: licet quidam eorum, non probantibus caeteris, dicant poenitentiam, ut & fidem, gratiam istam mereri de congruo: quoniam congruum & consentaneum est bonitati divinae, ut eam credentibus & poenitentibus benigne largiatur.
pass_a_gloss: And likewise, although they say that acts of repentance, fear, hope, and love are with the act of faith certain dispositions toward justification, they do not therefore understand works of that kind, properly speaking, either to effect or to merit justification. For they are not, on their mind, physical dispositions which by their own proper power effect or attain remission of sins and new righteousness: but only moral dispositions—that is, conditions which according to divine ordinance ought to precede in us the remission of sins and the gift of habitual righteousness, and without which God neither wills nor is wont to confer those benefits on a man, as may be seen in Peter of St. Joseph, Idea of Speculative Theology, book 4, chapter 9, Resolution 3. Nor even, as was proved above from the Council of Trent itself, do they attribute to any works the power of meriting the grace of justification, which, as the same Council notes, is not only remission of sins but also sanctification and renovation of the interior man: which remission and renovation all theologians of the Roman Church acknowledge to be merely gratuitous, and owed from justice to none of our acts or dispositions: although some of them, the rest not approving, say that repentance, as also faith, merits that grace de congruo—because it is fitting and agreeable to divine goodness that he kindly bestow it on believers and the penitent.
pass_b_english: Penitent acts with faith are moral conditions God requires—not physical causes that produce first grace.
Rome (mostly): remission and renovation remain mere gifts; a minority still speaks of congruous merit.
